SHALLOW.name: Splash Bomb Special
SHALLOW.description: A jerrycan wobbles out of the barrel, thuds down, and mostly just makes a mess.
SHALLOW.logic: The t-shirt cannon only cares that the jerrycan fits, so it lobs the sloshing can in a lazy arc. The gasoline's real property here is just its liquid mass — it splashes wide when it lands, leaving a slick puddle. The flare rides along unlit; no spark ever meets the spill, so there's no fire, just a wet, slippery footprint where the can landed.

effects.note: gasoline splash makes the footing slick

stages.note: the flare never catches; all you get is a sloppy puddle

SHALLOW.name: Gas Jug Bonk
SHALLOW.description: A full jerrycan sails downrange in a lazy arc and just... lands. No spark, no flare struck against it — the fuel splashes wide but never catches, so all that's left is a wet, heavy jolt.
SHALLOW.logic: The cannon only cares that the can fits the barrel, not that it's fuel — it lobs the jerrycan like any other payload. Gasoline 'splashes wide, soaks in, and stays' but needs a spark to claim the spill; with the flare unstruck, the liquid's mass is the only thing that connects. A heavy sloshing jug hitting someone is a shove, not a fire.

effects.note: Full jerrycan lands as dead weight, no ignition, just a wet shove.

stages.note: The spark never happens; only the splash's weight registers.

MEDIUM.name: Tailgate Torch
MEDIUM.description: The cannon sends the fuel can arcing downrange; it splits open on impact and the flare tucked against it catches the fumes instantly.
MEDIUM.logic: Gasoline's fumes catch before the liquid does, and one spark claims the whole spill — the flare, burning wet or dry regardless of the fall, is exactly that spark. Packed against the jerrycan, its open flame ignites the spreading puddle the instant the payload lands, turning a simple splash into fire right at the landing zone.

effects.note: gas splash slicks the ground on landing
the flare's flame catches the fumes as they spread

stages.note: a controlled catch, not a detonation

MEDIUM.name: Flashpoint Lob
MEDIUM.description: The can bursts the instant it lands — fumes catching on contact rather than waiting to soak in — and the flash off the ignition is bright enough to leave whoever's standing there seeing spots.
MEDIUM.logic: Gasoline fumes 'catch before the liquid does,' so read as an instant contact-ignition rather than a delayed burn: the moment the payload hits, the whole spill goes up at once instead of pooling first. The road flare's own property — 'bright enough to blind night eyes' — becomes the aftershock of that same ignition, the flash disorienting rather than marking. Two properties of the same spark, read as one sharp beat instead of a slow soak.

effects.note: Fumes catch on contact instead of pooling — the whole spill claims itself at once.

stages.note: Instant ignition, not a delayed burn.

effects.note: Flare-bright flash off the same ignition leaves them blinking and stumbling.

stages.note: The blinding brightness rides the same blast as its own aftershock.

DEEP.name: Bleacher Inferno
DEEP.description: It lands soft, splits wide, and for one heartbeat nothing happens — then the whole puddle goes up at once, and something keeps glowing in the wreckage long after.
DEEP.logic: The cannon doesn't discriminate about payload, so it throws the whole rig — jerrycan and lit flare together. On impact the gasoline does what it does best: splashes wide and soaks into the ground, spreading its reach past the point of impact. The fumes take a half-beat to reach the flare's flame, and because one spark claims the whole spill, that delay becomes a single unified ignition instead of a small burn — a real detonation. The flare itself burns wet or dry and survives the blast, its embers still glowing in the crater, bright enough to mark the position and pull stragglers toward the smoldering ground even as the main fire dies down.

stages.note: the puddle spreads before it ignites

DEEP.name: Firebreak Cannonade
DEEP.description: The can detonates on landing, punching outward and dragging up a wall of fire between you and them — and by the time the flames die down, the ground it burned into is a black, sticky mess that won't let go of anyone still standing on it.
DEEP.logic: Read gasoline not as a weapon payload but as a firewall: 'splashes wide, soaks in, and stays' describes a spill that covers ground, and the flare igniting it (burns wet or dry, wind be damned) turns that ground into a barrier, not just a burst — hence SHIELD at SELF, the wall standing between the thrower and whatever's downrange. The initial contact still knocks back and detonates, because fumes catch instantly. But gasoline that 'soaks in and stays' doesn't burn clean — once the flame exhausts the fuel it leaves scorched, tarry residue behind, which is read here as ground that grabs feet rather than ground that's simply gone black: a SNARE that only appears once the fire itself expires.

effects.note: Fumes catch instantly, the blast shoving outward on contact.
The whole spill claims itself the moment the flare's spark reaches it.

stages.note: Contact ignition, not a slow soak.

effects.note: The burning spill stands as a wall of flame between you and whatever's beyond it.

stages.note: A spill that soaks in and stays becomes a barrier, not just a burst.

effects.note: Burnt-out fuel leaves the ground tarry and sticky, grabbing at anyone still standing on it.

stages.note: The fire dies, but what it soaked into doesn't let go.

SHALLOW.name: Pool Boy's Payback
SHALLOW.description: A thin, bleachy jet that stings more than it hurts — the kind of spray you get when someone who cleans pools for a living finally snaps.
SHALLOW.logic: The pressure washer is locked as the beam's form: it turns a trickle into a cutting stream. Fed straight pool-shock granules with no water to activate them, the jet mostly just carries dissolved chemical dust — real, but weak, since the granules 'boil into fog' only when they have something proper to react with. Right now it's just a corrosive squirt: the obvious, low-effort reading of 'spray chemicals at target.'

effects.note: Chlorinated jet stings exposed skin and eyes on contact, barely more than an angry hose.

stages.note: A functional but underwhelming spray.

SHALLOW.name: Sneeze Shot
SHALLOW.description: You aim the wand expecting a cutting jet and get a cough of bleachy mist instead — the granules never fully dissolved, so all that comes out is a stinging, watery spray.
SHALLOW.logic: The pressure washer's cutting jet needs a solid stream to strip paint; here the chlorine granules clog and half-dissolve, so the beam that leaves the nozzle is weak, diluted fog rather than a real cutting stream. The only honest effect left is the eye-and-throat sting the dust is known for on its own — enough to make someone flinch, nothing more.

effects.note: diluted chlorine mist stings eyes and throat, forcing a flinch/sneeze

MEDIUM.name: Eyewater Special
MEDIUM.description: The washer's punch knocks you back a step, and by the time you catch your footing your eyes are streaming and your legs won't cooperate.
MEDIUM.logic: Two real properties chained in sequence: the pressure washer's stated ability to 'push heavy things back' becomes the first beat, a knockback on impact. Then the chlorine granules, agitated by the jet's moisture, boil into the stinging fog the tub promises — eyes and throat catching the brunt, read here as a lingering SLOW rather than raw damage, since the fog is described as irritating, not lethal on its own.

effects.note: Paint-stripping force of the jet shoves the target back on contact.

stages.note: The physical punch of the water.

effects.note: Chlorine dust reacts with moisture into stinging fog, blurring vision and fouling breath.

stages.note: The chemical follow-through.

MEDIUM.name: Bleach Line
MEDIUM.description: The washer does what a pressure washer actually does — throws a jet hard enough to strip paint and peel bark — except now it's carrying pool-shock granules, and the line it cuts keeps going through whatever's standing behind the first target.
MEDIUM.logic: Read the pressure washer for its real, unglamorous property: it's a paint-stripping, bark-peeling cutting jet, which as a beam naturally reads as something that punches through, not just knocks back. The chlorine riding in the stream adds the corrosive bite of granules that 'eat color, fabric, and skin given time' — here compressed into an instant abrasive sting on impact.

effects.note: paint-stripping jet force plus chlorine's skin-eating bite
the cutting stream keeps its line, punching through into whoever's standing behind

DEEP.name: The Deep End Bites Back
DEEP.description: It hits like a wall, then the mist starts eating. Whatever you drop in it doesn't just fall down — it keeps dissolving, and if it goes down for good, the fog it was carrying blows outward and takes the next poor soul with it.
DEEP.logic: Every stage traces to the same reaction chain the tub describes: 'given something to react with, the granules boil into stinging fog.' The washer supplies both the force and the water to trigger that reaction. Stage one is the honest paint-stripping punch of the jet. Stage two is the fog itself blooming on contact, corrosive over time exactly as chlorine 'eats color, fabric, and skin given time' — rendered as a lingering burn with reach, not an instant kill. Stage three honors the dust's stated effect on 'eyes and throat': even after the burn fades, the fumes leave the target stumbling. The final stage is the discovered consequence: a target that dies still carrying an unspent tub of boiling chemical ruptures outward, since the granules were never fully reacted — a last chemical burst that catches whoever's standing nearby, turning one corroded kill into the start of the next fight.

effects.note: The cutting jet lands with paint-stripping force.

stages.note: The blunt first hit.

effects.note: Granules meeting the jet's moisture boil into a spreading chemical fog that keeps eating at skin and fabric.

stages.note: The reaction kicks in.

effects.note: Even as the fog clears, streaming eyes and raw lungs leave the target stumbling.

stages.note: The lingering aftermath.

effects.note: Unspent chemical trapped in the corroded target ruptures outward, splashing fresh fog onto anyone nearby.

stages.note: The chain reaction's payoff.

DEEP.name: Last Rinse
DEEP.description: The beam cuts a wet, stinging line through everyone in it — and the granules riding the stream don't stop working once the water lands. Fumes leap between soaked targets, and whatever chlorine dries on skin or cloth seizes up stiff, gluing the fight in place.
DEEP.logic: This reading chains three real properties instead of one: (1) the washer's actual job — a jet hard enough to strip paint and peel bark — is read as a beam that pierces a line of targets, not just the first; (2) chlorine granules 'given something to react with... boil into stinging fog,' and the shared wet trail the beam leaves between soaked targets is exactly that reactive medium, so the fog arcs — chains — from one dripping target to the next; (3) the granules that 'eat color, fabric, and skin given time' don't finish reacting instantly — left on cloth and skin, the residue dries stiff over the following seconds, gumming movement like drying bleach-crusted fabric always does. Each stage is a real consequence of the last, not a bolted-on number.

the stream holds its line through multiple soaked targets
chlorine fumes ionize along the wet trail and arc to nearby soaked targets
residual chlorine dries stiff on skin and cloth, seizing movement like crusted bleach fabric

SHALLOW.name: Halfhearted Hallway
SHALLOW.description: A rolling fan wedged in the doorway kicks up a proud gust of wind... that mostly just stirs dust and barely nudges the marbles scattered underfoot.
SHALLOW.logic: The fan's real job is to shove airborne light stuff — mist, powder, sparks — down its lane. Marbles are solid glass, not airborne, so the obvious idea of blowing them at an intruder mostly fails; the wind can only jostle them a hair on the hard floor, leaving a token trip hazard instead of a weapon.

effects.note: marbles nudged just enough by the breeze to catch an ankle

stages.note: the fan's one honest trick fizzles into a stumble

SHALLOW.name: The Halfhearted Gale
SHALLOW.description: A drum fan wheezing in the doorway, doing its best impression of a weapon and mostly failing.
SHALLOW.logic: The fan's only stated power is a steady lane of wind that shoves loose junk downrange — with the marbles too heavy for airflow to move and the foam can never popped, that wind lane is the whole gadget. All it can honestly do is nudge someone light who wanders through it.

effects.note: the wind lane gives a token shove to anyone caught crossing the doorway.

stages.note: marbles stay inert on the floor, foam stays capped; the fan alone is a lot of noise for a small push.

MEDIUM.name: The Jammed Threshold
MEDIUM.description: A bead of foam sprayed straight into the fan's own housing swells and cures, seizing the whole rolling drum into a rock-solid plug wedged across the doorway — with a spill of marbles left underfoot from the setup.
MEDIUM.logic: Foam's stated property is that it becomes the new mechanism wherever it's sprayed; packed into the fan's works it seizes the moving parts and hardens into a fixed obstruction rather than a wind source. True to their nature, the marbles keep rolling loose around the base, so anyone forcing past the plug also has to fight their footing.

effects.note: cured foam seizes the fan drum into a solid plug blocking the doorway
loose marbles underfoot ruin the footing of anyone forcing through

stages.note: the leftover mess punishes whoever muscles past the plug

MEDIUM.name: The Bowling Lane
MEDIUM.description: The fan turns the doorway into a firing lane and the marbles into ammunition that refuses to stop rolling.
MEDIUM.logic: The fan's job is shoving loose junk downrange, and a bag of marbles is exactly that — loose, hard, and rolling. Blown at speed they become buckshot on the first person in the lane, and because marbles 'roll forever on any hard floor,' the survivors of the first hit keep skittering on to strike whoever's next in the corridor.

effects.note: the fan hurls the loose marbles down the lane like buckshot into the first body in the doorway.
glass marbles never stop rolling on hard floor, bouncing on to the next target in line.

DEEP.name: The Narrowing
DEEP.description: Foam swells around the fan's throat until only a thin gap remains; the wind that once ambled down the lane now screams through the choke point, and the marbles waiting in the mechanism get fired like glass buckshot — then left carpeting the floor for whoever follows.
DEEP.logic: The fan's lane pushes anything airborne with steady, dependable force. Foam cures rock hard exactly where it's sprayed, so packing it around the fan's throat doesn't block the lane outright — it narrows it, and the same air now has to move through a smaller gap, so it moves faster. Marbles, too heavy to ride an idle breeze, are exactly light enough to ride a breeze squeezed through a choke, so the narrowed jet turns them into an actual payload. Once fired, the marbles' true property — endless rolling on hard floors — becomes the last word: the floor itself, not the fan, is what finally ends the chase.

DEEP.name: The Settling Storm
DEEP.description: A marble barrage down a wind-forced lane that eventually goes quiet — and that quiet is when the real trap closes.
DEEP.logic: First the fan does what it does honestly: it shoves the loose marbles downrange as a weapon, and the marbles' endless rolling on hard floor turns one impact into a chain of hits down the corridor, staggering whoever's first hit by the sudden glass storm. But a thin bead of foam laid along the threshold before the fight was set to cure the whole time — tacky at first, then rock-hard. By the time the marble storm has spent itself and the rolling finally stops, the foam has finished curing and locks whoever's still standing in the doorway to the floor.

SHALLOW.name: Backyard Bruiser
SHALLOW.description: A trimmer whip with a pair of jumper cables dragging off the tip like dead weight — more clutter than circuit.
SHALLOW.logic: The weed whacker's spinning line is read at its most obvious: a line that stings and shreds anything soft on contact, delivered here as a whip. The jumper cables have no live source to bridge to, so their bite-and-hold trait never triggers; they just add inert mass to the swing, occasionally fouling the line's motion. The result is a plain, unremarkable lash.

effects.note: the whipping trimmer line stings and shreds on contact, nothing more

stages.note: the cables contribute nothing; the reading fails to find anything past the obvious sting

SHALLOW.name: Fence's Length
SHALLOW.description: A stinging arc of trimmer line keeps anyone who gets close at exactly a pole's length, the dangling cable clamps just dead weight on the swing.
SHALLOW.logic: The weed whacker's core property — it keeps threats at a full pole's length — reads here as a simple shove, nothing more. The jumper cables have no live source to bridge, so the clamps just hang inert, adding swing weight but doing nothing electrical. Obvious, mildly functional, that's all.

effects.note: the spinning line's reach shoves anything that strays inside it back to arm's length

MEDIUM.name: Clampjaw Cord
MEDIUM.description: The line still snaps like a weed whacker gone rogue, but the copper clamps riding its tip snag whatever it wraps around and refuse to let go.
MEDIUM.logic: The whip's shredding property leads the hit as ordinary damage. The jumper cables' stated trait — 'the clamps bite onto anything and hold' — activates the moment the line wraps a target, converting the lash's tail-end contact into a literal clamp-down, holding the struck target in place after the strike.

MEDIUM.name: Copper Drag
MEDIUM.description: The whip's line lashes out and the trailing clamps snap shut on whatever it catches, insulated cord dragging behind and fouling their footing.
MEDIUM.logic: Jumper-cable clamps genuinely bite onto anything and hold — that becomes the snare. The long insulated leads that trail from the whip's tip are heavy and tangle-prone; wrapped around a caught limb they don't cut, they drag, reading as a slow rather than damage. No live source means no shock, so this stays a pure control tool, not a weapon.

DEEP.name: The Grid Bites Back
DEEP.description: The whip cracks, the clamps at its tip snag flesh and lock on, and for one crackling second the target becomes a live node in someone else's circuit — the charge doesn't stop with them, and when it collapses, it comes home.
DEEP.logic: Stage one is the whip doing what a shredding trimmer line does, but the jumper-cable clamps at its tip realize their stated bite-and-hold property on the wrap, snaring the struck target instead of just stinging them. Stage two takes the cables' other core trait seriously: bridged to a live source, anything conductive they're clipped to becomes part of the circuit — so the held target completes a circuit that arcs outward, chaining the charge to other nearby conductive targets and staggering them with the jolt. Stage three follows the logic of the insulated leads carrying current both ways: when the clamped target goes down, the collapsing circuit has nowhere else to go but back down the line into the wielder's hands, surging them with a burst of speed from the discharge.

the clamps bite onto the struck target and hold, per their stated grip
the clamped target becomes part of the circuit; charge jumps to nearby conductive targets

DEEP.name: The Recoil Line
DEEP.description: The whip snags a target in copper jaws, the wielder yanks the taut cable and sends them cartwheeling skyward, and when the clamps finally let go the stored recoil snaps back as a buffer around the wielder.
DEEP.logic: Stage one is the clamps' most basic truth — they bite onto anything and hold — read as a snare. Stage two reads the whip's shaft and the taut insulated cable together as a single lever: a spinning-line whip already swings its tip with real momentum, and yanking a cable pinned to something transfers that swing into a violent upward jerk, launching the snared target rather than cutting them. Stage three is just physics catching up — what goes up on a whip-line comes down hard, staggering them on landing. Stage four reads the insulated leads literally: they're built to carry and contain charge without leaking it to the handler, so when the snare finally releases, that contained tension/charge discharges outward as a brief protective buffer for whoever's holding the cord. No blade ever bites here, so no damage effect belongs — this whole reading is leash, sling, and shock-absorber, never a cutter.

SHALLOW.name: Just a Gun
SHALLOW.description: You point it, you pull the trigger, something gets hit. That's the whole trick.
SHALLOW.logic: The delivery is a standard 9mm pistol and the ammo is a plain box of 9mm rounds — inert cartridges that only do what any matching firearm does once fed. There is no hidden property here, no twist to read into cardboard and brass. The honest reading is the boring one: it fires, it hits, that's the extent of it.

effects.note: A standard round doing standard round things. No flourish.

stages.note: The obvious, unimaginative outcome of pistol plus bullets.

SHALLOW.name: The Old Standby
SHALLOW.description: You point, you pull the trigger, and something happens — just not much. The sidearm does its job and the round does its job, but neither one does anything else.
SHALLOW.logic: The pistol is stated to be a plain sidearm with nothing clever about it, and the rounds are inert cargo until fed — so read literally, all this junk delivers is a shove of mass at speed. No piercing, no burn, just the bullet's blunt momentum making someone stumble.

MEDIUM.name: Point and Click
MEDIUM.description: The shot lands and the recoil-transfer through the target's frame knocks them half a step sideways before the sting even registers.
MEDIUM.logic: 9mm rounds carry real momentum on impact — enough to jolt a body even without dramatic stopping power. Reading past 'bullet hurts you' into 'bullet also shoves you' is the mild cleverness here: the pistol's mundane hitscan snap becomes a two-beat hit, sting then stumble.

MEDIUM.name: Fast Hands
MEDIUM.description: A simple sidearm loaded with simple rounds rewards a simple truth: nothing about this gun asks you to think, so you can move faster than someone who has to.
MEDIUM.logic: The pistol's stated lack of complexity — 'nothing clever about it' — is itself a property: a dead-simple action means no fumbling, no cycling delay, just point and go. The box of rounds being ready-fed removes hesitation from the follow-up shot. That mechanical simplicity becomes a self-buff, and the round still lands with its genuine stopping power on the target.

DEEP.name: Clean Through
DEEP.description: The round doesn't stop at the first thing it meets — it punches clean through, and if that first thing drops, the leftover momentum finds a second target before you've even eased off the trigger.
DEEP.logic: A 9mm round is a small, fast, low-drag projectile — it's known for overpenetrating thin or soft targets rather than stopping dead in them, which is the truer property under 'it just shoots.' Reading the box of rounds as capacity rather than ammunition explains the follow-through: there's always another cartridge chambered, so a kill doesn't end the sequence, it continues it — the spent round's exit energy is read as carrying into whoever's standing behind, and the shooter's hand is already resetting for the next trigger pull.

DEEP.name: Second Wind
DEEP.description: The bullet is not just lead — it's a tiny controlled fire. It burns going in, the wound stiffens as it cools, and if the shot finishes someone off, the shooter feels it too: a jolt that makes the next draw feel effortless.
DEEP.logic: A 9mm round is a metal jacket around burning propellant — that combustion is a real, if unstated-until-now, property of 'a box of 9mm rounds,' and it means the impact carries heat, not just force. The wound that heat leaves behind cools and stiffens afterward, slowing whatever it's in. And because the pistol is described as doing exactly what a pistol does — nothing more, nothing hidden — the only place left for surprise is in the shooter's own reaction to a clean kill: a rush that, for a few seconds, makes them faster on the draw. SHALLOW.name: The Rusty Bite
SHALLOW.description: A bear trap staked under a scatter of leaves, doing exactly what a bear trap does: something steps wrong, and it stops stepping.

The oil jug sits untouched nearby; motor oil needs heat or a slicked stretch of ground to matter, and here it's just poured too thin and too late to do anything but stain the leaves. SHALLOW.name: Oops, My Foot
SHALLOW.description: A rusty jaw waits under a spreading dark stain. Step in it and instead of clamping shut, your foot skids right off the greased steel.

MEDIUM.name: Slip 'n' Snap
MEDIUM.description: A ring of dark, gleaming oil circles the hidden trap — step anywhere near it and your feet go first, then the jaws finish the job.

Poured in a ring around the staked trap, it turns the approach into a skating rink, so anything that stumbles into the slicked zone loses its footing before ever reaching the jaws, which then do their one honest job: clamp and hold.

MEDIUM.name: Whiplash Grease
MEDIUM.description: The jaws snap, but the oil under them turns the bite into a violent slingshot — up, back, and then nowhere fast.
MEDIUM.logic: The spring is loaded to snap hard enough to hold — that stored force doesn't vanish just because the oil ruins the grip. It has to go somewhere, so it launches the caught limb and knocks the rest of the body backward instead of clamping down. What the jaws leave behind is the oil film, which keeps footing bad long after the trap lets go.

DEEP.name: The Grease Fire Waltz
DEEP.description: Leaves hide the jaws, oil hides the floor. Something steps in, the trap bites down — and the spark off steel teeth meeting steel teeth turns the whole slicked stretch into a sheet of fire.
DEEP.logic: Every property of both objects is chained in the order they'd actually happen. The oil is poured across the floor for its stated use — turning the stretch into a skating rink — but it's also flammable once something gets it hot enough, and clings in a film rather than pooling thin. The trap's steel jaws, snapping shut with spring-loaded force, are the exact kind of hard metal-on-metal impact that throws sparks. So: the victim slides into the trap (the oil doing its job), the jaws clamp shut (the trap doing its job), the impact spark catches the oil clinging to both the victim and the ground, and the fire doesn't stay put — it runs along the same slicked stretch the oil was poured across, catching anyone else standing in the film. What's left after the fire burns itself out is a scorched, still-slick patch that keeps tripping people long after the flames are gone.

DEEP.name: The Good Samaritan Special

MEDIUM.name: The Backfire Bottle
MEDIUM.description: Breaks like any bottle would — but the foam riding inside wasn't finished hissing when the glass split it open, and that hiss doesn't go out quietly.
MEDIUM.logic: Reads the foam not as a solid loaf but in its stated wet, uncured state — a thin bead that's still full of aerosol propellant before it swells. The bottle's shatter delivers the initial glass-shard damage as usual, but the friction and impact energy of that same shatter now has something flammable to ignite, so the propellant trapped in the still-tacky foam catches and smears a shallow burn across the wound. The rounds remain honestly inert — no rifle, no fire — just added heft in the glob.

effects.note: glass shards on impact
uncured foam's propellant ignites from the shattering friction, smearing a low burn

DEEP.name: The Bullet Piñata
DEEP.description: It looks like a busted bottle and a bad smell. It is actually a slow-setting trap with a fistful of rifle rounds baked into the shell — hit it again and it lets go all at once.
DEEP.logic: The glass does what glass does — it shatters and splashes its payload wide, and the foam inside doesn't just spray, it swells around whatever it hits and starts curing from tacky to rock, per its own stated behavior. The 5.56 rounds, poured into the bottle alongside the foam, aren't inert weight anymore — they're rebar. As the foam sets rock-hard around the target, it locks the rounds into the shell with it. That shell holds until it's struck again: another impact cracks the cured foam, and the trapped rounds and glass splinters go off as shrapnel, with the pressure still caught in the swollen foam kicking the target backward as it lets go.

the burst of expanding foam shoves before it grips
the shell finishes curing to rock, weighing the target down

stages.note: the cure finishes a moment later

effects.note: a hit on the cured shell cracks it, and the rounds baked inside spray out as shrapnel
the trapped expansion pressure kicks free all at once

stages.note: only fires if the encased target is struck again

DEEP.name: The Late Payment
DEEP.description: Doesn't look like much when it lands — a wet slap, a scratch, a dud. Give it a few seconds. The can wasn't finished swelling.
DEEP.logic: Chains all three objects across time instead of at once. The bottle's shatter delivers the small, honest first hit — glass doing what glass does. But the foam's stated behavior is that it keeps swelling after it's sprayed and only cures from tacky to rock in place over time — it doesn't stop reacting just because the bottle already broke. The 5.56 rounds, inert without a rifle to fire them, get folded into that spreading, hardening loaf as nothing more than dense loose chunks. As the foam keeps expanding against its own hardening crust, the shell can't hold the pressure — it splits, and the trapped rounds get kicked out as shrapnel, turning a 'failed' throw into a delayed second payload nobody watching would have called.
